Dispatch

Dispatch does not exist in because state changes are not triggered by sending indirect messages to a central store. Instead, state transitions are produced by executing a deterministic pipeline that resolves intent into a finalized state snapshot.

In dispatch-based architectures, state updates are initiated by emitting actions into a store, where external reducers, middleware, and side effects interpret those actions and eventually mutate or replace state. This model relies on indirect messaging and deferred interpretation.

takes a different approach: state changes are the result of pipeline execution, not the outcome of dispatching commands. Engineers do not dispatch instructions — they submit values, promises, or behaviors to a pipeline that deterministically produces a single, authoritative state snapshot.

doesn’t need dispatch because intent, execution, and state commitment are already unified. When a pipeline runs, it resolves exactly once, commits exactly once, and emits a finalized, immutable state snapshot through the Vault.

Why There Is No Dispatch Layer

Dispatch-based systems separate intent (actions) from execution (external reducers and middleware). Actions are broadcast into a system that decides how — or whether — state should change.

does not support this indirection. All state transitions are explicit, scoped, and executed through a FeatureCell pipeline. There is no global action bus, no external reducer fan-out, and no implicit mutation triggered by message dispatch.

Instead of dispatching actions, engineers invoke pipeline entry points such as replaceState or mergeState. These APIs submit concrete inputs into the pipeline, where resolve, operator, filter, and policy stages execute deterministically before state is committed.

Recommended References

  • Pipeline Overview — how intent flows through the system
  • Resolve Stage — where async and deferred inputs are handled
  • State Stage — how finalized snapshots are committed and emitted

Engineers migrating from dispatch-based systems should treat pipeline entry APIs as the replacement for dispatch, and pipeline stages as the replacement for external reducers and middleware.

Submitting Intent in SDuX

Although does not have dispatch, engineers still express intent to change state. That intent is submitted directly into the pipeline as concrete input rather than as an abstract action.

This shifts state updates from a message-based command model to an execution-based resolution model. Instead of broadcasting “what happened,” engineers provide “what should be resolved,” and the pipeline deterministically produces the outcome.

Because pipeline execution is explicit and scoped to a FeatureCell, state changes are predictable, isolated, and easier to reason about. There is no ambiguity about which external reducers ran, which middleware intercepted an action, or whether execution short-circuited.

Note

intentionally avoids a global dispatch or action layer. Introducing one would require additional indirection, implicit routing rules, and shared mutable concerns that undermine the pipeline’s determinism and isolation guarantees.

By submitting intent directly into the pipeline, keeps state transitions explicit, auditable, and bound to a single execution boundary.

Examples: Submitting Intent Without Dispatch

In dispatch-based architectures, state changes are triggered by sending actions into a store. In , state changes occur by executing the pipeline with a concrete input. There is no dispatch step.

The examples below demonstrate how engineers submit intent directly into a FeatureCell pipeline using replaceState. In all cases, intent is submitted directly into the pipeline. The Resolve stage executes the deferred input, the pipeline completes deterministically, and the State stage commits a single authoritative snapshot — without dispatch, external reducers, or action interpretation.

Example: Execute the Pipeline Without Dispatch
